name: Grain shortage in Hatti
what: Hittite kings beg Egypt and Ugarit for grain; one letter calls a shipment a matter of life or death.

name: Seaborne raiders strike the Levant and Egypt
what: From Merneptah's Year 5 to Ramesses III's Year 8, Egyptian texts and Ugarit's last letters record raiders arriving by sea.

name: Ramesses III fights the Sea Peoples
what: Battles on land and in the Nile mouths in Ramesses III's eighth year, carved on his temple at Medinet Habu.

name: Earthquake storm in the eastern Mediterranean (proposed)
what: A proposed half-century run of large earthquakes that damaged Mycenae, Troy, Ugarit and other centres.

name: Foot soldiers beat chariot armies (Drews' thesis)
what: Robert Drews' claim that skirmishers with javelins and long Naue II swords made the palace chariot corps obsolete.

name: Late Bronze Age palace trade network
what: Copper from Cyprus, tin from Afghanistan, grain from Egypt and royal gifts tied Hatti, Egypt, Babylon, Mycenae and Ugarit together; the Uluburun wreck carried about ten tons of copper.

name: Egypt loses its Levantine empire
what: After Ramesses III, Egyptian garrisons in Canaan disappear and the Philistines settle the southern coast.

name: Linear B writing falls out of use
what: With the palaces gone, the Greek-speaking world loses writing for about four centuries.

name: Greek Dark Age
what: Fewer and smaller settlements, no palaces, no writing, and a much reduced population in Greece.

name: The Phoenician alphabet spreads
what: A 22-letter script used by merchant cities such as Byblos and Tyre spreads around the Mediterranean.

name: Neo-Assyrian expansion begins
what: Adad-nirari II starts the campaigns that make Assyria the first Iron Age empire.

name: Cyprus rebounds after the collapse
what: Cypriot towns such as Kition rebuild and keep trading copper while the palaces elsewhere stay dead.

name: Younger Dryas cold snap
what: A return to near-glacial cold and drought for about 1,200 years at the end of the Ice Age.

name: The Holocene begins
what: A warmer, wetter and above all steadier climate than any in the previous 100,000 years.

name: Natufian foragers settle down
what: Hamlets of stone houses in the Levant where people harvested wild cereals and stored food before farming.

name: First farming villages of the Fertile Crescent
what: Pre-Pottery Neolithic villages cultivate wheat, barley and pulses and later herd sheep, goats and cattle.

name: Early farmers grow shorter and sicker
what: Skeletons of early farmers show more tooth decay, anaemia, growth arrest and infection than those of foragers.

name: Neolithic population boom
what: Farmers have children faster than foragers, so farming populations grow even as health worsens.

name: Foragers raise the enclosures of Göbekli Tepe
what: Carved stone pillars up to about 5 metres tall, set up by people who did not yet farm.

name: Ubaid temples at Eridu grow into ritual centres
what: Successive temples rebuilt on the same spot become the seat of a hereditary priestly elite.

name: Canal irrigation in southern Mesopotamia
what: Short canals off the Euphrates turn the alluvium into the most productive grain land of its day.

name: The first state forms at Uruk
what: A city of perhaps 25,000 to 50,000 people with temples, ration lists, bureaucrats and a ruler.

name: Uruk colonies spread up the Euphrates
what: Southern Mesopotamians found outposts such as Habuba Kabira to tap timber, metal and stone.

name: Rival chiefdoms of Upper Egypt fight
what: Naqada, Hierakonpolis and Abydos compete along a valley hemmed in by desert.

name: Egypt unified under the First Dynasty
what: The Nile valley from the Delta to the First Cataract becomes one kingdom.

name: Trypillia mega-sites
what: Planned settlements of perhaps 10,000 people in Ukraine with no palaces, temples or signs of rulers.

name: The Axial Age
what: Jaspers' name for the centuries that produced Confucius, Laozi, the Buddha, the Upanishads, the Hebrew prophets and Greek philosophy.

name: First coins struck in Lydia
what: Electrum coins at Sardis; coinage appears in the Ganges valley and China within about a century.

name: Second urbanization of the Ganges plain
what: Iron tools, rice surpluses and cities such as Rajagriha and Shravasti grow in the age of the Buddha.

name: Warring States boom in China
what: Iron tools, mass infantry armies, cities, markets and bronze coins across north China.

name: Archaic Greek boom
what: Colonies, trade and larger houses: Greek living standards rise fast after the Dark Age.

name: Egyptian ma'at, a moral order upheld by kings
what: Truth, justice and cosmic order that the pharaoh must uphold, two thousand years before the Axial Age.

name: The summer monsoon weakens over northwest India
what: Lake and river records show less summer rain over the Indus plains from about 4,100 years ago.

name: Ghaggar-Hakra rivers dwindle
what: Monsoon-fed rivers between the Indus and the Yamuna shrink to seasonal streams.

name: Late Harappan villages move east
what: Settlement shifts from the great cities to many small villages in Haryana and the Ganges-Yamuna doab.

name: Violence and disease rise in Late Harappan burials
what: Skulls from Harappa's late cemeteries show more head wounds, leprosy and tuberculosis.

name: Gulf trade with Meluhha fades
what: Indus seals, beads and weights stop reaching Mesopotamia; Meluhha drops out of the texts.

name: Ancestral North Indians form
what: Ancient DNA shows people of Indus Periphery ancestry mixing with steppe newcomers after the cities declined.

name: Roman Transitional Period: a less stable climate
what: After the Roman Climate Optimum, more variable weather, weaker Nile floods and episodes of drought.

name: Roman silver and lead mining slumps
what: Lead pollution in Greenland ice falls sharply in the 160s and stays low for centuries.

name: Roman silver coinage collapses
what: The silver content of the antoninianus falls to a few percent; prices soar.

name: Diocletian's reforms
what: More provinces, a larger army and a new tax system based on regular assessments of land and people.

name: Constantine's gold solidus
what: A gold coin struck at 72 to the Roman pound that stayed stable in the East for some 700 years.

name: Constantinople's long-distance water supply
what: The Valens Aqueduct and hundreds of kilometres of Thracian channels feeding cisterns inside the walls.

name: Goths cross the Danube
what: Tens of thousands of Tervingi and Greuthungi, fleeing the Huns, enter Roman Thrace.

name: Treaty of 382 settles the Goths in the Balkans
what: Theodosius settles the Goths inside the empire as allies under their own leaders.

name: Vandals, Alans and Sueves cross the Rhine
what: Several barbarian groups cross near Mainz and over the next years reach Gaul and Spain.

name: Visigoths settled in Aquitaine
what: The Western government settles Wallia's Goths in the Garonne valley.

name: Usurpations and court wars in the West
what: Constantine III, Stilicho's fall, Aetius against Boniface, Ricimer's puppet emperors: the West spends its army on itself.

name: The Western treasury shrinks as provinces are lost
what: Britain, much of Spain and Gaul, and then Africa stop paying taxes to the emperor in Italy.

name: The great expedition against Vandal Carthage fails
what: A joint East-West armada is burned by Vandal fireships off Cape Bon.

name: Material collapse in the post-Roman West
what: Fewer and cruder pots, coins and roof tiles, smaller cattle; in Britain the economy drops below Iron Age levels.

name: Holy men, bishops and monks remake Mediterranean culture
what: Peter Brown's late antiquity: a creative world of saints, monasteries and new elites, not only a decline.

name: The East keeps a rich, compact tax base
what: Egypt, Syria and Anatolia were the empire's richest farmland and lay behind the Bosporus, far from the Rhine and upper Danube.

name: Long Roman-Persian peace in the East
what: After Armenia was partitioned around 387, the two empires fought only briefly until 502.

name: Constantinople pays Attila off in gold
what: Treaties of the 430s and 440s buy peace from the Huns with growing annual payments of gold.

name: Leo I has the general Aspar killed
what: The Eastern court breaks the hold of an Alan-Gothic generalissimo and leans on Isaurian troops instead.

name: Justinian's wars of reconquest
what: Belisarius takes Vandal Africa in a year; the Gothic war in Italy drags on for two decades.

name: Lombards invade Italy
what: Three years after Justinian's death the Lombards take most of northern Italy from the empire.

name: The last great Roman-Persian war
what: Persia takes Syria, Palestine and Egypt and reaches the Bosporus before Heraclius strikes back.

name: Persians take Egypt and Constantinople's free bread ends
what: The loss of Egyptian grain ends the public bread distribution in the capital.

name: Constantinople survives every siege for eight centuries
what: Huns, Goths, Avars, Persians, Arabs and Bulgars all fail to take the city until the crusaders of 1204.

name: The army is settled on the land in the themes
what: After the Arab conquests, field armies withdraw to Anatolian districts and live off local resources.

name: Great families absorb land and tenants
what: Locally powerful lineages build estates, shelter dependants from the census and dominate local office.

name: The Qiang wars
what: Rebellions of Qiang peoples in the northwest that cost the Later Han treasury billions of cash.

name: Later Han treasury and tax registers shrink
what: Frontier wars, disasters and hidden households leave the court short of money and men.

name: Proscription of the Partisans
what: Palace eunuchs ban hundreds of reform-minded scholar-officials from office.

name: Epidemics in Later Han China
what: The histories record repeated great pestilences in the second half of the second century.

name: Cooler, drier late second century in north China (proposed)
what: Proxy and documentary records reviewed by Fan Ka-wai point to colder conditions as Han fell.

name: The Yellow Turban rebellion
what: Zhang Jue's Way of Great Peace raises hundreds of thousands across eastern China in one spring.

name: Dong Zhuo seizes the court and burns Luoyang
what: A frontier general takes the capital after the palace massacre of 189 and moves the court west to Chang'an.

name: Cao Cao's military farm colonies
what: Refugees and soldiers settled on abandoned land around Xu feed Cao Cao's armies.

name: The last Han emperor abdicates
what: Emperor Xian yields the throne to Cao Pi, who founds the Wei dynasty.

name: China splits into three kingdoms
what: Wei in the north, Shu in Sichuan and Wu on the Yangzi each claim the mandate.

name: Jin conquers Wu and reunites China
what: A brief reunification that lasts barely a generation.

name: Xiongnu forces sack Luoyang
what: The Yongjia disaster: the Jin capital falls and north China passes to non-Han dynasties for almost three centuries.

name: Philip II builds a new Macedonian army
what: Pike phalanx, heavy Companion cavalry and a siege train, paid for with Thracian gold.

name: Bagoas poisons two kings and Darius III takes the throne
what: Artaxerxes III and his son Artases die within two years; a royal cousin becomes Darius III.

name: Bessus murders Darius III
what: Fleeing Alexander, the Great King is stabbed by his own satraps.

name: Alexander turns the Persian hoards into coin
what: Ancient writers put the bullion taken at Susa and Persepolis at well over 100,000 talents; much was minted to pay armies.

name: Alexander keeps Persian satraps and court ways
what: Persian nobles stay as governors, tribute systems continue and the king adopts Persian dress and ceremony.

name: Wars of Alexander's Successors
what: Forty years of war among Alexander's generals split the empire into kingdoms.

name: Iron smelting at Meroe
what: Slag heaps around the royal city record centuries of iron production.

name: Rome and Kush at war, then at peace
what: Kushite raids on Roman Egypt, a Roman punitive march to Napata, and a treaty at Samos that was generous to Kush.

name: Kush trades with Roman Egypt
what: Two and a half centuries of mostly peaceful exchange along the Nile frontier.

name: Adulis becomes Aksum's port on the Red Sea
what: Ivory, tortoiseshell and rhinoceros horn go out; cloth, metal, wine and oil come in from Roman Egypt and India.

name: Aksum strikes its own gold coins
what: From King Endubis, Aksum issues gold, silver and bronze coins with Greek legends.

name: Noba settle in the Meroitic heartland
what: Newcomers associated with the Noba of the Aksumite inscriptions spread along the Nile.

name: Ezana campaigns against the Noba on the Nile
what: Ezana's inscription claims victories at the junction of the Nile and the Atbara.

name: Kaleb of Aksum invades Himyar
what: An Aksumite army crosses the Red Sea to overthrow the Jewish king of Himyar.

name: Soil erosion around Aksum (Butzer's thesis)
what: Butzer read slope deposits as signs of deforestation and overused fields near the capital.

name: Aksum's Red Sea power fades
what: Coinage stops, Adulis declines and the kingdom's centre moves south into the highlands.
